purpose: Pyridostigmine is most commonly used to treat myasthenia gravis, a condition where the muscles become weak and tire easily. It helps improve muscle strength so you can perform everyday activities like swallowing, breathing, and moving more easily. It has also been used in the military as a protective agent and occasionally for other muscle-related conditions.
how_it_works: Your muscles work when nerve signals tell them to contract, and a chemical called acetylcholine carries those signals. In myasthenia gravis, those signals are blocked and the acetylcholine breaks down too quickly. Pyridostigmine slows down the breakdown of acetylcholine, so the signal stays strong longer and your muscles can work better.
common_side_effects: You may notice increased saliva, sweating, or tears. Stomach cramps, nausea, diarrhea, or vomiting are fairly common. Some people experience muscle twitching, a runny nose, or more frequent urination. These effects usually mean the medication is working but may be uncomfortable.
warnings: Too much of this medication can cause a cholinergic crisis, which means the muscles become overly stimulated and can actually get weaker — this is a medical emergency. Tell your doctor right away if you notice sudden increased weakness, trouble breathing, severe vomiting, or excessive secretions. Tell your doctor about all your other medications, especially heart medications, since pyridostigmine can slow your heart rate. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor.
typical_dosing: For myasthenia gravis, the usual starting dose is 30 to 60 mg taken by mouth every 3 to 4 hours while you are awake, often 3 to 4 times a day. Your doctor will adjust the dose based on how your muscles respond. A long-acting overnight tablet (180 mg) is sometimes given at bedtime. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes, since the right dose is very individual.
